q: On March 1, a client sells 500 shares of XYZ at a $10,000 loss. On March 20, she buys 500 shares of XYZ again because she still wants the position. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The loss is deductible only if she waits 60 days before repurchasing
The loss is treated as a capital gain because the repurchase increases her holdings
The $10,000 loss is fully deductible this year because the sale and purchase happened in the same tax year
The loss is disallowed under the wash-sale rule and is added to the basis of the repurchased shares
rationale: Wrong — the rule uses a window of 30 days on each side of the sale, so waiting until day 31 would be needed, not 60 days.
Wrong — a repurchase does not convert a loss into a gain; the loss is deferred through basis adjustment.
Wrong — the wash-sale rule applies within 30 days before or after a sale, regardless of tax year boundaries, so the loss is not deductible.
Correct — repurchasing substantially identical stock within the 61-day window disallows the loss and adds it to the basis of the new shares.
explanation: Wash-sale: a loss is disallowed if substantially identical securities are bought within 30 days before or after the sale. The disallowed loss adjusts the basis of the replacement shares.

q: A client has $12,000 of net capital losses for the year and $0 in capital gains. Her taxable income is $80,000 from wages. Which statement about how the loss is used is correct?
choices: Up to $3,000 offsets ordinary income this year, and the remainder carries forward to future years
Nothing can be used, because capital losses only offset capital gains
The loss expires at the end of the year if unused
The full $12,000 offsets her wages this year
rationale: Correct — up to $3,000 of net capital loss offsets ordinary income each year, and the rest carries forward indefinitely.
Wrong — capital losses can offset up to a set amount of ordinary income, so they are not limited to capital gains.
Wrong — unused capital losses do not expire; they carry forward until used.
Wrong — net capital losses offset ordinary income only up to an annual limit, not without limit.
explanation: Net capital loss deduction against ordinary income is limited to $3,000 per year ($1,500 for married filing separately), with an indefinite carryforward.

q: A client bought stock on January 15, 2025, and sold it on January 20, 2026. How should the gain be characterized?
choices: Short-term, because it was sold in the same calendar year as the new year began
Long-term, because the holding period exceeded one year
Short-term, because the holding period must be measured by calendar years, not days
Long-term, but only if the stock paid a qualified dividend
rationale: Wrong — the holding period is measured from purchase to sale, not by calendar year.
Correct — the holding period runs from the day after purchase, and more than one year qualifies the gain as long-term.
Wrong — the holding period is measured in days and months from purchase, not in calendar years.
Wrong — dividends do not determine the holding period of the shares; the gain's character depends on the holding period.
explanation: Long-term capital gain: asset held more than one year. The holding period starts the day after the acquisition date.

q: A married couple files jointly with modified adjusted gross income of $300,000. Their net investment income is $40,000. What is their net investment income tax under the 3.8% rule?
rationale: Wrong — the couple's MAGI exceeds the joint threshold, so the tax applies.
Wrong — $1,900 applies 3.8% to $50,000, which is the excess of MAGI over the threshold, but the tax is limited to the lesser of net investment income or the excess.
Correct — the tax is 3.8% of the lesser of net investment income ($40,000) or MAGI above $250,000 ($50,000), which is $1,520.
Wrong — $11,400 applies 3.8% to total MAGI, but the tax base is only net investment income or the excess above the threshold.
explanation: NIIT = 3.8% × the lesser of (a) net investment income or (b) MAGI above the threshold ($200,000 single, $250,000 MFJ; these thresholds are not indexed).

q: A single taxpayer lived in her home for 23 of the last 60 months before selling it at a gain. Which statement about the Section 121 exclusion is correct?
choices: She qualifies for a partial exclusion only if she was employed in another city
She qualifies only if she rented the home out for the other months
She qualifies for the full exclusion, because the test is about the total time she owned the home
She does not qualify for the exclusion, because the ownership-and-use test requires 24 months within the 5 years before the sale
rationale: Wrong — employment-related partial exclusions exist under specific rules, but they are not what this scenario turns on, and she has not met the basic test.
Wrong — renting out the home does not satisfy the use test for the exclusion.
Wrong — the test looks at ownership and use within the five years before the sale, not total ownership time.
Correct — the standard two-of-five test requires at least 24 months of ownership and use within the five years before the sale; she falls short.
explanation: Section 121: $250,000 single or $500,000 MFJ exclusion, with at least 2 of the last 5 years of ownership and use. Partial exclusions exist for certain unforeseen circumstances.

q: A 16-year-old has $5,000 of unearned income from investments and no earned income. Under the kiddie tax rules, which statement is most accurate?
choices: The unearned income above the annual threshold is taxed at the parents' marginal rate
All of the income is taxed at the parents' marginal rate, regardless of amount
The income is tax-free because the child is a minor
All of the income is taxed at the child's rate, which is typically zero
rationale: Correct — under the kiddie tax, unearned income above the annual threshold is taxed at the parents' marginal rate.
Wrong — only the amount above the threshold uses the parents' rate, not the entire amount.
Wrong — a child's unearned income is not exempt because the child is a minor.
Wrong — the first amount is taxed at the child's rate, but unearned income above the threshold is taxed at the parents' rate, so not all of it is at zero.
explanation: Kiddie tax applies to children under 19 (or under 24 full-time students) with unearned income above a threshold, which is taxed at the parents' marginal rate.

q: A client inherits stock from her father. His basis was $20,000, and the stock was worth $90,000 on the date of death. She sells the stock immediately for $90,000. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: She recognizes a $70,000 short-term capital gain
She recognizes no gain or loss, because her basis is stepped up to the date-of-death value
She recognizes a $20,000 gain, the father's original basis
She recognizes a $70,000 long-term capital gain
rationale: Wrong — the holding period of inherited property is treated as long-term, and the gain would be zero in any case.
Correct — inherited property generally takes a basis equal to its fair market value at death, so a sale at that value produces no gain.
Wrong — the father's original basis is replaced by the stepped-up basis for inherited assets.
Wrong — the basis is adjusted to the date-of-death value, not kept at the father's original cost.
explanation: Under IRC §1014, inherited property takes a basis equal to fair market value at death. Traditional IRA balances do not receive this step-up.

q: A client has a traditional IRA with a total balance of $100,000, of which $20,000 is after-tax basis from nondeductible contributions. She converts $20,000 to a Roth IRA this year and has no other IRA balances. How much of the conversion is taxable?
rationale: Wrong — the basis is only a fraction of the total IRA balance, so most of the conversion is taxable.
Wrong — $4,000 is the nontaxable portion. The taxable share is the larger 80%, or $16,000.
Correct — under the pro-rata rule, 20% of the conversion is nontaxable ($4,000) and 80% is taxable ($16,000).
Wrong — the nontaxable after-tax portion is excluded from income, so not all of the conversion is taxable.
explanation: Pro-rata rule: all traditional IRAs are aggregated. The nontaxable share equals after-tax basis divided by total IRA value, applied to the amount converted.

q: A client sells a property with an adjusted basis of $200,000 for $500,000. She receives $125,000 in the first year and a note for the rest, with payments in later years. Which statement about the first-year gain is correct?
choices: $125,000, because the entire down payment is recognized as gain
$300,000, because the full profit is recognized at closing regardless of payments
$60,000, because the profit percentage is applied to the note balance
$75,000, found by applying the gross profit percentage to the year-one payment
rationale: Wrong — the down payment is not all gain; only the gross profit percentage of it is recognized.
Wrong — under the installment method, gain is recognized as payments are received, not all at closing.
Wrong — the profit percentage applies to cash received, not to the note balance.
Correct — the gross profit percentage is $300,000 / $500,000 = 60%, and 60% of the $125,000 received is $75,000.
explanation: Installment method: gain each year = payments received in the year × gross profit percentage. Depreciation recapture is recognized in the year of sale regardless of payments.

q: A client's modified adjusted gross income is $130,000. He actively participates in a rental property that produces a $30,000 loss and has no other passive income. Under the special allowance rules, how much of the loss can he deduct this year?
choices: $10,000, because the $25,000 allowance is reduced by 50% of MAGI above $100,000
$0, because rental losses are never deductible against wages
$30,000, because all rental losses are deductible for active participants
$25,000, because the full special allowance applies at any income level
rationale: Correct — the allowance is $25,000 minus 50% of MAGI above $100,000 = $25,000 - $15,000 = $10,000, and the other $20,000 is suspended.
Wrong — active participants can use a limited allowance against nonpassive income.
Wrong — the active-participation allowance is capped at $25,000 and is reduced at higher income levels.
Wrong — the allowance phases out above $100,000 of MAGI, so the full $25,000 is not available here.
explanation: Active-participation rental allowance: $25,000, reduced by 50% of MAGI above $100,000 and fully phased out at $150,000. Disallowed losses carry forward.

q: A client wants to exchange a valuable painting she holds for investment for another painting, deferring the gain under a like-kind exchange. Which statement is correct?
choices: The exchange qualifies, because both assets are artwork and therefore like-kind
The exchange does not qualify, because like-kind treatment under Section 1031 applies only to real property
The exchange qualifies only if the paintings are held for at least ten years
The exchange qualifies if the client receives cash in the transaction
rationale: Wrong — artwork is personal property, and Section 1031 no longer covers personal property after 2017.
Correct — since 2018, like-kind exchange treatment under Section 1031 is limited to real property held for investment or business use.
Wrong — the holding period does not change the outcome; personal property is excluded from Section 1031 regardless.
Wrong — receiving cash does not make a personal-property exchange eligible; it may trigger recognition of gain.
explanation: The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act limited Section 1031 to real property. Exchanges of art, equipment, and other personal property no longer qualify.

q: A 72-year-old client has not yet reached her required beginning date for RMDs. She wants to make a qualified charitable distribution (QCD) from her IRA. Which statement is correct?
choices: She can make a QCD, but the amount is fully taxable and does not count toward any RMD
She cannot make a QCD until she reaches the RMD age
She can make a QCD now, because QCDs are available from age 70½, and the amount generally excludes from income
She can make a QCD only if she itemizes deductions
rationale: Wrong — a QCD is excluded from income, not taxable, and it counts toward her RMD once that requirement applies.
Wrong — QCDs begin at age 70½, which is earlier than the RMD age, so she qualifies.
Correct — a QCD from an IRA can be made from age 70½, and the distribution is excluded from taxable income up to the annual limit.
Wrong — a QCD is an exclusion from income, so it works whether or not she itemizes.
explanation: QCD: from an IRA, age 70½ or older, paid directly to a qualifying charity; excluded from income up to the indexed annual limit, and counts toward any RMD.

q: A client gives her adult child $50,000 in cash this year. She has made no other taxable gifts. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The full $50,000 is subject to gift tax at a 40% rate
The gift is tax-free and does not need to be reported, because it is cash
No gift tax return is required, because the gift is under $100,000
A gift tax return is required, the first $19,000 is excluded, and the $31,000 excess reduces her lifetime exemption without tax due
rationale: Wrong — gift tax applies only to the amount above the lifetime exemption, not to every dollar of the gift at a flat 40%.
Wrong — cash gifts are not exempt, and gifts above the annual exclusion must be reported.
Wrong — the threshold for a gift tax return is any gift above the annual exclusion, not a $100,000 figure.
Correct — the 2026 annual exclusion is $19,000 per recipient, so the $31,000 excess is reported on Form 709 and uses part of the lifetime exemption, with no tax owed.
explanation: Gifts above the annual exclusion require Form 709 but generally do not trigger tax until the lifetime exemption is used up.

q: A client sells a collectible coin held for three years at a long-term gain. Which statement about the federal rate on that gain is correct?
choices: The gain is taxed at a maximum rate of 28%, which is higher than the top long-term rate for most other assets
The gain is taxed at 3.8%, the net investment income tax rate, and no income tax applies
The gain is taxed at the 0%, 15%, or 20% long-term rates, the same as stock
The gain is taxed at ordinary income rates, with no preferential treatment
rationale: Correct — long-term gain on collectibles is taxed at a maximum rate of 28%, which can exceed the 20% rate that applies to most long-term gains.
Wrong — the 3.8% NIIT is an additional tax on top of the income tax, not the rate on the gain itself.
Wrong — collectibles do not get the standard long-term rates that apply to most capital assets like stock.
Wrong — collectibles have a specific long-term maximum rate, so they do not simply follow ordinary rates.
explanation: Long-term gain on collectibles (art, coins, antiques, precious metals in many cases) is taxed at a maximum 28% rate.

q: A retired client receives $30,000 of Social Security benefits and $20,000 of other income, including $10,000 of tax-exempt municipal bond interest. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Municipal bond interest is excluded when calculating how much of the Social Security benefit is taxable, so it has no effect
Municipal bond interest is added to provisional income, which can cause more of the Social Security benefit to be taxable
Municipal bond interest is taxable, so it is treated the same as ordinary income for all purposes
Social Security benefits are never taxable when the client has tax-exempt income
rationale: Wrong — tax-exempt interest is included in provisional income for Social Security taxability, even though it is not taxed directly.
Correct — provisional income includes tax-exempt interest, which can raise the taxable share of Social Security benefits.
Wrong — municipal interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, although it counts in the Social Security calculation.
Wrong — the exemption of other income does not remove Social Security taxation, which depends on provisional income.
explanation: Provisional income = AGI (without SS) + tax-exempt interest + 50% of SS benefits. Tax-exempt interest increases the amount of benefits that may be taxable.
